CargoLedger · Smart Invoicing Module

One invoice.
Two teams.
Zero shared truth.

Operations and Accounts billed through spreadsheets, email, and re-typing. I turned that handoff into one shared invoicing workflow - billing errors fell from ~10% to under 0.5%.

Billing used to travel between two teams before it could become an invoice. Now it moves along one path, and the ERP is the last step rather than a re-typing job.

01 · THE PROBLEM

Billing was a game of telephone.

One invoice, one slow lap between two teams, and one wrong field restarted it. I mapped the workflow before designing anything. The delay was a handoff problem, not a screen problem.

Operations
Type into Excel
DO and container numbers, by hand.
→
Operations
Email the sheet
Spreadsheet sent to Accounts.
→
Accounts
Re-key and draft
Copy out, add GST and surcharges.
→
Accounts
Email back to check
Operations verifies the draft.
→
One wrong number
Rejected
Start over from scratch.
The insight both teams pointed to

Operations optimised for shipment accuracy. Accounts optimised for billing accuracy. The shared spreadsheet forced both into one workflow that served neither, and while the file bounced around, finished work sat unbilled.

Two teams ran one billing workflow with no shared record, so every invoice depended on hand-copied data and a single re-keyed digit could restart the cycle.

02 · UNDERSTANDING THE WORKFLOW

I built my understanding from the FRD and project discussions.

I didn’t directly interact with Operations or Accounts. My understanding came from the FRD, BA and PM discussions, and documented requirements. Instead of treating the FRD as screens to design, I focused on understanding who was involved, how information moved, and where errors were likely to happen.

What the FRD described

ROLE 01

Operations

Entered and verified cargo details like DO numbers, container numbers and shipment data before an invoice could proceed. Missing or incorrect data could send the draft back for correction.

ROLE 02

Accounts

Reviewed and validated the prepared invoice before processing it further. Any earlier mistakes often surfaced here, causing rework.

Key workflow issue

The main challenge wasn’t the number of fields, but the fact that validation happened across different stages, often by different people than those who entered the data. This created a loop:

Enter data → Validate → Find error → Send back → Fix → Re-validate

So the interface needed to do more than display data. It needed to help users catch issues early and understand what needs attention.

What this meant for the UI

FOCUS 01

Clear hierarchy for key information

So users can quickly scan and verify important details.

FOCUS 02

Clear and actionable error states

So users immediately understand what’s wrong and where to fix it.

FOCUS 03

Clear invoice status

So users always know an invoice’s state: in progress, needs correction, ready, or rejected.

This became the foundation for the screens I designed. My role was primarily UI-focused: translating the documented workflow into a clear interface, defining hierarchy and states, and ensuring consistency across the product.

03 · THE DIRECTION

From an email relay to one live record.

The direction was simple: replace a fragmented handoff with one shared invoice record, with each role responsible for the part they actually know. Instead of moving spreadsheets, emails, and copied data between teams, the system would carry the same record from request to invoice.

The new architecture · one record, four responsibilities

TRANSPORTERExternal · raises the request
01 · TRANSPORTER

Billing parties are defined at the start

An Empty Reuse Request cannot be submitted until the payer for each charge is identified. The information that was previously resolved later in the process is captured while the transporter has the context.

Lift-Off→assigned entity
Lift-On→assigned entity
Street-Turn→assigned entity
OPERATIONSInternal · confirms the physical movement
02 · OPERATIONS

Operations validates the operational record

The team works with the information they own: container reuse, delivery details, and movement status. The process removes the need to copy operational data into spreadsheets and send it to Accounts.

✓ No spreadsheet handoff · No email to finance · No duplicate data entry
SYSTEM · ZOHOAutomated · carries the record forward
03 · SYSTEM · ZOHO

Verified information moves directly into the invoicing system

Shipment details, billing parties, and calculated tax are passed to the invoicing backend automatically. The handoff is no longer a person carrying information from one system to another.

✓ No row misalignment · No ID typos · No manual re-keying
ACCOUNTSInternal · validates and commits
04 · ACCOUNTS

Accounts reviews the numbers instead of rebuilding them

Rate cards, surcharges, and GST are calculated before the invoice reaches Accounts. Their role shifts from manually preparing the invoice to reviewing the figures, validating them against the contract, and committing the invoice.

One action→invoice generated

Three principles shaped the direction

01

Shift-left attribution

Before

Billing-party ambiguity was resolved late in the process, often after the physical job was complete.

The direction

Capture the payer when the request is created, while the person with the relevant context is making the request.

02

Decoupled responsibilities

Each role owns a clearly defined part of the record.

Transporter

Defines the billing parties.

Operations

Confirms the physical movement.

Accounts

Validates the financial information and commits the invoice.

The interface should make these boundaries visible rather than asking one team to compensate for another.

03

Automated synchronisation

The system carries verified information between stages instead of relying on people to copy it.

This removes manual handoff points where errors can be introduced and allows Accounts to focus on validation rather than transcription.

The design implication

This direction changed what the interface needed to do. It wasn’t just a matter of making the existing invoice screens cleaner. The UI needed to make ownership, status, validation, and exceptions visible at every stage of the record.

That became the foundation for the design.

04 · THE DECISIONS

Three structures explored. Four decisions shaped the final module.

I explored three possible structures and discussed their implications with the PM and BA. The shared-record approach aligned best with the workflow requirements. From there, four decisions shaped how the module worked.

One invoice, two internal readswhat shape should the product take?
One mega-tableeverything, for everyone, at once
✗ REJECTED

Simple to build and easy to keep in sync, but it recreated the overload: cargo detail drowned Accounts, while tax detail overwhelmed Operations

Two separate modulesone module per team, synchronised between them
✗ REJECTED

Each team gets a focused workspace, but the relay remains: two places to maintain, two places that can drift, and another reconciliation point

One record, two readsshared data, role-specific views
✓ SELECTED

One underlying record, with focused views for each team. More UI to maintain, but one source of truth and no manual re-keying between views

Why this direction won

The rejected structures solved one problem while recreating another. The mega-table reduced duplication but brought back information overload. Two separate modules reduced cognitive load but recreated the handoff between teams. The shared-record approach addressed both: one source of truth underneath, focused experiences on top.

01

One shared source of truth

The same record, not another version

ProblemThe documented workflow showed information moving through spreadsheets, emails, and separate records, creating opportunities for versions to diverge.
DecisionStructure the experience around one shared invoice record that could be consumed by both teams and ultimately passed to the ERP.
Trade-offA shared record means that incorrect information affects everyone. We therefore made ownership and provenance visible wherever it mattered.
ResultBoth teams work from the same underlying information instead of reconciling separate versions.
02

Two reads, not two systems

Focus the interface without splitting the data

ProblemThe same record contains very different kinds of information. Cargo detail is important to Operations but largely noise for Accounts; tax and billing detail work the other way around.
DecisionCreate two tailored views on the same data model rather than separate modules or one permission-heavy dashboard.
Trade-offTwo views mean more UI to maintain. We kept them on a shared component foundation so patterns could remain consistent across both.
ResultEach team sees the information relevant to its responsibility without creating a second source of truth.
03

Preview before commit

Replace the hidden review step with an explicit one

ProblemRemoving the email-based handoff also removed an informal review point that existed before an invoice was committed.
DecisionIntroduce a mandatory preview with per-line GST, expandable calculation details, and flags for rates that deviate from the client contract.
Trade-offIt adds an extra step to every invoice. We accepted that friction because the action creates a financial document.
PrincipleBetter to slow down at the gate than correct an invoice after it leaves the system.
ResultPotential issues are surfaced before the invoice is committed.
04

Honest ERP integration

Design for failure, not the happy path

ProblemAn invoice is not complete until it synchronises with Zoho Books - a system outside the product’s control.
DecisionShow synchronisation status at the row level and provide a retry action when a sync fails.
Trade-offA failed state makes the interface look less polished. Hiding it would make the experience feel cleaner but leave Accounts without visibility into what actually happened.
PrincipleIf the system can fail, the interface should make the failure visible and recoverable.
ResultAccounts can identify and retry failed synchronisations without relying on an invisible handoff.
Constraints the decisions had to work within
  • Zoho Books was fixed. The ERP integration could not be redesigned.
  • GST was non-negotiable. HSN, CGST, and SGST had to be supported at line level.
  • Upstream data quality was outside our control. The UI had to handle incomplete or incorrect job information.
  • Scope was deliberately limited. Credit notes, partial payments, and multi-currency were parked for a later phase.
  • Ten weeks, sole designer. The solution had to balance product quality with what could realistically be designed and delivered within the project window.

05 · THE STRUCTURE

The skeleton, before any colour.

With the direction set, I moved into structure: what each surface needed to accomplish, what information belonged together, and how one step led to the next.

Four core surfaces defined the flow.

01The queue

Requests waiting to be invoiced, with charge type and amount visible directly in the row. The goal: help users find the work before deciding what to do with it.

02The create step

Bill-to, charge types, and invoice format sit alongside the requests being selected. The goal: keep the grouping decision close to the records it affects.

03The record

Operational context sits above the invoice details, with charges, line-level tax, billing summary, and synchronisation status organised into a single view. The goal: let users move through the record from context → charges → validation → commit.

04The sync ledger

Status counts provide an overview, followed by one row per invoice with its current synchronisation state. The goal: make integration failures visible at the list level instead of burying them inside individual records.

Structure before styling

I kept the wireframes deliberately neutral at this stage. The focus was not colour, polish, or visual treatment. It was whether the right information appeared in the right place, whether the hierarchy supported the workflow, and whether each surface handed the user naturally into the next one.

Colour, component states, and visual styling came later.

06 · THE DESIGN SYSTEM

One library behind both views.

Once the structure was established, I defined the visual system before detailing the individual screens.

The goal was simple: Operations and Accounts should feel like two views of the same product, not two separately designed interfaces.

The Figma library became the shared foundation for colour, typography, spacing, states, and components.

07 · THE SCREENS

The same record, read two ways.

Operations works with the physical movement. Accounts works with the money. Both views are built on the same underlying record, with the interface changing according to what each role needs to see and do.

The visual language was designed for long, information-dense working sessions: compact tables, restrained colour, clear hierarchy, and status that stays visible.

Open the Figma file ↗

The dashboard

Status first. Detail second. Invoice status becomes the organising idea of the dashboard: paid, pending, overdue and draft.

The proportions give an immediate sense of what is happening before any individual record is opened.

01 · The queue

Find the work before deciding what to do with it. The queue holds completed jobs ready to move into invoicing, and the default view surfaces enough to act on without opening every record: billing party, charges, amount, date and status.

One row per request, readable without opening anything.

Filters support the deeper searches: branch, party, date, charge type.

Sorting stays an explicit labelled control rather than hiding inside column headers. Sort order decides what gets worked first, so it should read as a deliberate action.

02 · The create step

Make the grouping decision explicit. Cargo and delivery orders are pulled from the existing job record, so Operations selects what should be invoiced rather than re-entering it. Invoice format is presented as an explicit choice with a sensible default, and the total updates as the selection changes, keeping the consequence of that decision visible.

Add invoice · format as an explicit choice

Nothing selected. The summary and primary action stay visible but inactive, so what will happen is legible without committing an incomplete selection.

Count and total update in the footer as the selection changes, so the scope of the invoice is always in view.

Split by DO, the default. Requests sharing a DO pair group into one invoice per charge type.

Individual. One invoice per request and charge type, for clients who reconcile line by line.

By container. Grouping driven by container rather than delivery order.

No charges. An honest dead end. The screen says why nothing can be invoiced instead of showing an empty table under a live button.

03 · The gate

Preview before anything becomes an invoice. This is Decision 03 made visible. There is no direct create action on the selection screen, so the workflow forces a preview before anything is committed, and the primary action names the quantity rather than saying submit: Preview 3 invoices.

Preview. Three invoices split by charge type, each showing HSN/SAC per line, tariff and applicable tax, the line-level calculation, and a subtotal that reconciles against the bill summary. If something is wrong, Modify Selection is the reversible path back.

The last reversible moment before a financial document exists.

04 · The record

The same job, now read as money. The record brings operational context and financial detail into one place, and each charge expands to show how the amount was calculated rather than asking anyone to trust a final number.

Invoice details. HSN/SAC sits alongside each charge rather than being buried elsewhere. CGST and SGST are shown separately at line level, with both rate and amount visible. Billing party carries the full entity name, GST number and address from the original request. These are not decorative details: they are the fields that decide whether an invoice moves forward or comes back for correction.

From decision to interface

The final UI is a direct reflection of the decisions made earlier.

One shared record→Operations and Accounts work from the same underlying information.
Two reads→Each role gets the information and actions relevant to its responsibility.
Preview before commit→The invoice cannot be created without passing through an explicit review step.
Honest ERP integration→Synchronisation state is visible instead of hidden behind the workflow.

08 · THE STATES

The happy path was the smallest part of the work.

A production workflow has more than success and failure. Sync can fail. Filters can return nothing. Upstream data can change. Tax rules can reject a payload.

Decision 04 established the principle:

If the system can fail, the interface should make the failure visible and recoverable.
Invoices listing · one surface, five states

Ready
Validated and available to download.

Invoiced
Generated and synced. The terminal success state.

Pending sync
Queued for Zoho. This state exists so a delay never looks like a failure.

Error
The invoice number reads Not yet generated rather than sitting blank, and every row carries two actions: retry, and open the log.

Empty
Nothing matches the filters, stated plainly, with the way back.

When the sync fails, say why

A failed integration usually reaches finance as “something went wrong.” Here the request and the response are both in the interface.

API logs. Timestamped attempts with status. The failed call expands to show the payload and the reason: 400 · “Apply IGST for interstate transactions.” That sentence tells an accountant exactly what to fix, in their own vocabulary. Without it the same failure becomes a support ticket and a phone call.

Refresh re-pulls the operational record when upstream details change.

Resend is confirmed rather than fired silently.

09 · THE HANDOFF

I handed the front-end team a foundation, not a picture.

After design sign-off I built the HTML/CSS front-end structure myself and handed it to the front-end team as the implementation base. The markup followed the same component structure as the Figma library, so the relationship between design components and front-end components was clear from the start.

Design → code

FigmaTokens · components · variants · states
↓
HTML/CSS foundationStructure · responsive behaviour · reusable patterns
↓
Front-end teamIntegration · data binding · system behaviour

I walked the front-end team through the structure and the design decisions behind it during handoff. Integration into the application was theirs.

Why this mattered

Building the front-end foundation myself meant implementation constraints surfaced during design delivery rather than after it. If a component, layout, or interaction was difficult to build, I could resolve it while the design context was still fresh.

So the handoff was not design → throw over the wall → build. It was a connected path from design system → UI structure → implementation.

10 · THE RESULT

Fewer handoffs, fewer opportunities for error.

The design was built to remove manual handoffs from the invoicing workflow and move validation closer to the point where information enters the system.

Some outcomes were designed into the product. The business measured the error reduction after launch.

Designed outcomes

DATA ENTRY
No manual re-keying

Cargo information is carried forward from the job record and tax is calculated by the system, removing an entire class of errors at the point of entry rather than asking users to catch them later.

SHARED WORKFLOW
One shared record

The invoice no longer travels as a spreadsheet or email attachment between teams. Both views work from the same underlying record.

SPEED TO BILL
Same-day creation

Once Operations logs the required cargo information, the invoice workflow can begin without waiting on someone to forward the next file.

ACCOUNTABILITY
Every value has context

Ownership and source are visible where it matters, so instead of asking which version is current, both teams work from the same record.

ERP VISIBILITY
Synced · Zoho Books

Synchronisation status is visible at invoice level with a retry path when something fails, so finance can see what happened without relying on an invisible integration.

FAILURE
A named, recoverable state

A sync failure carries its reason and its recovery action inside the product, instead of staying hidden until someone discovers an invoice never reached the ERP.

BUSINESS-MEASURED OUTCOME · AFTER LAUNCH
~10% → <0.5%
Billing errors and complaints

Per the internal business audit comparing periods before and after launch, billing errors and complaints fell from approximately 10% to below 0.5%. That is roughly 100 issues per 1,000 requests becoming fewer than 5.

The mechanism

Enter→Validate→Preview→Commit

Errors that previously surfaced later in the process could be caught before the invoice reached the customer.

What changed

The remaining errors were primarily associated with the billing party being selected incorrectly when the request was first raised. That matters because the failure moved upstream to a single, identifiable decision point, which is a smaller and more actionable problem than the distributed errors created by the previous workflow.

The business impact

The new workflow also creates the potential for faster cash conversion by shortening the gap between job completion and invoice creation. I would track average days-to-pay as the next live business metric.

The design can shorten fulfilled → invoiced. The business can then measure what happens to invoiced → paid. That distinction matters: the first is a product outcome we designed for, the second requires ongoing business data to prove.

We replaced a chain of manual handoffs with one shared record, moved validation upstream, and made failures visible before they became someone else’s problem.

11 · REFLECTION

What the project taught me, and what I would measure next.

01

How I would prove it worked

The next step would be instrumenting the workflow rather than relying only on the post-launch audit. I would track edits at preview, deviation flags, post-sync rejections, sync failures, and days-to-pay.

More issues caught at preview → fewer issues after sync

I would pay particular attention to the Zoho integration. The retry experience is designed, but volume-based error telemetry would show whether the recovery path actually holds up in production.

02

What being the sole designer meant

It was not about designing every screen alone. It meant maintaining one consistent thread from business requirement to workflow to interface to design system to implementation, and being responsible for making sure that thread did not break as the work moved between design, product, and engineering.

03

How building the front end changed my design

Writing the HTML/CSS foundation myself made implementation constraints part of the design process earlier. Component reuse, responsive behaviour, states, and feasibility were considerations from the beginning rather than problems discovered at handoff.

What used to be a handoff conversation became part of the initial design decision.

04

The lesson I keep

The real product was never the invoice screens. It was getting two teams, each holding part of the information, to trust one shared record.

That changed how I think about enterprise products: good UI does not just help people complete a task, it makes the system trustworthy enough for people to rely on.
